A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable 20-page versions of the same DirectLayout work. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across appendix reordering.

before.justification: v1 reports original scene-generation comparisons and ablations in Tables 1–2, with qualitative results and alignment examples in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds human evaluation in Section 4.4/Table 3 and inference-time measurements in Appendix D/Table 4.

M1.justification: The BEV generation, 3D lifting, iterative alignment, CoT supervision, dual evaluators, and DPO training procedure remain unchanged. The reward equations are consolidated into equivalent expressions; the suggested replacement of asset generation with retrieval is not presented as an implemented method change.

E1.justification: Both versions retain 3D-Front training, DPO descriptions spanning 40 scene categories, and 45 evaluation cases across 15 categories with coarse, medium, and fine prompts. Human scoring and timing measurements add evaluation procedures without documenting new scene domains, generation tasks, or input scenarios.

E2.justification: LayoutGPT, I-Design, and Holodeck remain the external comparators; the QwQ-BEV variant and original ablation configurations are also retained. The new human and timing comparisons reuse the existing external baselines. 'IDesign' in Table 4 is the existing I-Design comparator.

E3.justification: Section 4.4 introduces randomized, anonymized human evaluation by 25 compensated volunteers with relevant professional expertise, scoring three quality criteria across prompt granularities. Appendix D adds timing over 30 samples under stated consistent hardware and network conditions. These substantially extend evaluation design, while existing training and automated evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The reward and task-decomposition ablations, QwQ substitution analysis, qualitative examples, and iterative-alignment case study are retained unchanged. The added studies provide comparative human-quality and latency measurements without introducing new ablations, sensitivity tests, robustness tests, or error analyses.

E5.justification: Table 4 newly reports runtime minima and maxima alongside averages over 30 samples, adding descriptive variability reporting; DirectLayout ranges from 109.45 to 298.13 seconds. These are ranges across samples, not confidence intervals or repeated-seed uncertainty. Human-rating uncertainty and significance tests remain unreported.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial human-rating and timing results. Table 3 favors DirectLayout at every granularity; its fine-prompt scores are 4.84/4.72/4.80 versus I-Design's 3.32/3.72/2.72 for semantic compliance/physical plausibility/layout rationality. Table 4 reports average times of 185.24 seconds for DirectLayout, 5.87 for LayoutGPT, 166.86 for I-Design, and 210.23 for Holodeck. These are new measurements, not improvements over v1 under matched settings.

T1.justification: The layout definitions, validity ratios, entropy weighting, and iterative update remain mathematically equivalent. v2 moves the validity-ratio equation inline, corrects the criterion-index typo, and substitutes the existing weights into the reward expression. No substantive mathematical definition, assumption, derivation, or proof changes.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and main conclusion retain the same claims about direct numerical generation, CoT-based spatial reasoning, physical plausibility, semantic alignment, and fine-grained control. The new evaluations support these existing claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's latency and model-capacity limitations, v2 identifies training-data scale/diversity, difficulty generating many small objects, and reduced BEV clarity for vertically stacked objects. Appendix D also attributes substantial runtime to asset generation and discusses retrieval or faster generators as possible remedies.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds an approximate Trellis asset-generation cost of 26 seconds per object and describes the timing measurement scope. Existing prompts, training hyperparameters, GPU specifications, training times, and the project link remain unchanged. No new code or data availability is documented.

R1.justification: The same 36 cited works and related-work positioning are retained. Reference 15 updates Proc-GS from its arXiv entry to CVPR 2025, which is a publication-metadata update for the same work.

P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites and condenses the reward explanation, adds user-study and timing sections, expands limitations, and reorders appendices. It also adds funding acknowledgments and updates affiliation numbering and the publication header. Most existing prose and the overall narrative remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 3–4 for human evaluation and timing, reflows the conclusion and references, and repositions appendix material and Figures 5–6. All six original figures and the original comparison and ablation table designs are retained.

improvement.justification: The added randomized, anonymized human evaluation provides useful corroboration beyond automated metrics, while runtime measurements and specific small-object and vertical-stacking limitations improve transparency. The gains are bounded by incomplete user-study reporting: the rating scale, number of rated layouts, and uncertainty of human scores are unspecified. Overall, v2 strengthens validation and qualification of the unchanged method.
